criterion_notes.c1: Examines household drinking-water service access in Mbour, Senegal, including piped connection to the Sénégalaise Des Eaux (SDE) distribution network, use of standpipes and wells, water affordability, and daily water consumption volume.
criterion_notes.c2: Fails both the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading of Criterion 2. Plain reading: Although the abstract makes a one-phrase passing assertion about 'integration issues at the governance level' and 'the perverse effect of the reform of the Senegalese water sector in 1995' (PDF Page 1), and the conclusion notes in a single descriptive sentence that standpipe water costs 1,750 CFA francs/m3 versus the 191 CFA francs/m3 SDE social rate (PDF Page 7), the paper does not empirically examine any legal, administrative, institutional, regulatory, or governance factor; instead, it maps household income poverty and spatial location on a 500 m GIS grid to propose a decision-support mapping tool for municipal officials. Narrow 2026-10-13 reading: Even if passing references to the 1995 sector reform, SDE social tariff, or municipal decision-support GIS tools were treated as touching governance broadly, none is operationalized or analysed as a rule-type mechanism governing access (unanalysed macro-governance/tariff background and generic GIS decision-support tool development).
criterion_notes.c3: Empirical cross-sectional study combining Kompsat satellite imagery, systematic 500 m spatial grid household survey data (120 households, 99.19% response rate), water invoice/container volume measurements, and stakeholder interviews processed in SPSS and ArcGIS.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports multiple household water access outcomes: piped connection to the SDE distribution network (48.7%), well usage (38.6%), water poverty/affordability (>5% of monthly household income spent on water, affecting 52.4% of paying families), and daily per-capita water volume (Water Access Index in m3/person/day).
criterion_notes.c5: Population and unit of analysis (households in Mbour across 500 m grid cells, n = 120), the study's own analysed exposures/correlates (household income poverty <600 CFA francs/day and spatial location), outcomes, and cross-sectional spatial survey design are identifiable, though no eligible legal/administrative exposure is examined.

raw_response.exposure: Household income poverty (<600 CFA francs/day) and spatial/neighborhood location across a 500 m urban grid (no legal, administrative, regulatory, or governance factor empirically examined)
raw_response.outcome: Household connection to the SDE piped water distribution network (48.7%), well-water reliance (38.6%), water affordability/water poverty (>5% of monthly income spent on water), and daily per-capita water volume (Water Access Index, m3/person/day)
raw_response.population_and_sample: Households in the coastal town of Mbour, Senegal; n = 120 households sampled via a 500 m regular spatial grid (99.19% response rate, representing >1,000 inhabitants), supplemented by interviews with water company and government officials
raw_response.rationale: Excluded under E03 (Wrong exposure). While this empirical GIS-based household survey in Mbour, Senegal (n = 120 households) measures household water service access outcomes (piped SDE connection, well use, water expenditure >5% of income, and daily per-capita water volume), its empirical analysis examines only spatial variation and correlations with household income poverty (<600 CFA francs/day) to demonstrate GIS mapping as a municipal decision-support tool. Passing remarks about the 1995 Senegalese water sector reform in the abstract and standpipe vs. social-rate prices in the conclusion are unanalysed background statements with no empirical evaluation of any legal, administrative, regulatory, or governance mechanism.
raw_response.study_design: Cross-sectional spatial grid household survey with GIS thematic mapping and key-informant interviews
